nodes.title: Wikipedia: Pedometer ('10,000 steps')
nodes.claim: Repeats 10,000 steps a day as the standard walking recommendation, documents the origin as Kato's manpo-kei 'ten-thousand step-meter', and notes most health benefit is obtained by around 7,000 steps per day.
nodes.note: Layer-1 amplifier: canonizes the number while quietly embedding its marketing origin; living page (snapshot verified Sep 2026).

nodes.title: How walking 10,000 steps a day changes your body
nodes.claim: Promises body transformations from walking 10,000 steps a day over 3 months while conceding the target was 'a marketing ploy that dates back to a Japanese pedometer brand in the 1960s' and suggesting 7,500 steps may suffice.
nodes.note: Typical modern hype node: debunk caveat in passing, 10,000 kept in the headline and goal.

nodes.title: You Don't Need to Walk 10,000 Steps Every Day
nodes.claim: Reports that 10,000 steps is 'the default daily goal for some of the most popular activity trackers on the market' despite tracing the figure to Yamasa's 1965 marketing pedometer, and notes mortality rates level off at about 7,500 steps.
nodes.note: Names the tracker-default mechanism that cemented the number on millions of wrists.

nodes.title: U of T 10,000 Steps Challenge for Staff
nodes.claim: Month-long staff wellness challenge (May 1-31, 2024, run with Incentfit) in which teams win prizes by averaging 10,000 steps per day.
nodes.note: Workplace-challenge variant: the product number institutionalized as HR wellness policy.

nodes.title: '10,000 Steps Duesseldorf' campaign
nodes.authors: Fialho et al. (Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act)
nodes.claim: Evaluates the '10,000 Steps Duesseldorf' city-wide campaign promoting 10,000 steps/day (627 participants at baseline); intervention participants walked only ~462 more steps/day than controls and rates of actually reaching 10,000 did not differ.
nodes.note: The mutation scaled to municipal policy: a city program named for a pedometer slogan, with no origin science cited.

nodes.title: Yamasa 'Manpo-kei' pedometer
nodes.claim: The 10,000-steps figure began as 'Manpo-kei' (ten-thousand-steps meter), the name of Yamasa's 1965 pedometer launched around the 1964 Tokyo Olympics fitness boom - a marketing slogan, not a scientific finding; Harvard Health confirms 'the name was a marketing tool.'
nodes.note: True origin of the number: a Japanese product name recast worldwide as a clinical commandment (origin documented by Harvard Health, Jul 2019).

nodes.title: Step volume & intensity vs mortality in older women
nodes.authors: Lee IM et al. (JAMA Intern Med)
nodes.claim: Among 16,741 women (mean age 72) wearing accelerometers, more daily steps were associated with lower all-cause mortality until approximately 7,500 steps/day, with no further mortality benefit beyond that point.
nodes.note: First large cohort to show the mortality plateau sits ~25% below the folk target. JAMA Intern Med 2019;179(8):1105-1112.

nodes.title: Daily step count & mortality in US adults (NHANES)
nodes.claim: Among 4,840 US adults aged 40+, a greater daily step count was significantly associated with lower all-cause mortality, with benefit concentrated around 8,000 steps/day versus ~4,000; step intensity was not associated with mortality after adjustment for step volume.
nodes.note: National-sample cohort evidence that the benefit concentrates well below 10,000. JAMA 2020;323(12):1151-1160.

nodes.title: Daily steps & all-cause mortality: 15-cohort meta-analysis
nodes.authors: Paluch E et al. (Lancet Public Health)
nodes.claim: Across 47,471 adults in 15 international cohorts, more steps per day were associated with progressively lower all-cause mortality up to about 6,000-8,000 steps/day for adults aged 60+ and 8,000-10,000 for younger adults, with no special additional benefit at 10,000 itself.
nodes.note: Definitive dose-response meta-analysis: 10,000 was never a threshold. Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228.

nodes.title: Steps per day & mortality in middle age (CARDIA)
nodes.authors: Paluch E et al. (JAMA Netw Open)
nodes.claim: Among 2,110 Black and White men and women aged 38-50 in the CARDIA cohort, taking approximately 7,000 steps/day or more was associated with lower mortality than taking fewer than 7,000, with mortality rates leveling out at higher step counts.
nodes.note: Strong cohort evidence sitting entirely outside the hype chain - cited by none of the popular layer. JAMA Netw Open 2021;4(9):e2124516.
